title: Imports and Module Structure
content: This file builds directly on CentralLimitTheoremOQ01OQ02, which defines gaussianExponent μ σ_sq t = ↑(μ*t) * I − ↑(σ_sq * t²/2). The imports pull in Mathlib's Complex number arithmetic (Complex.Basic), special functions (Circle), and Lean tactics. The open declarations bring Complex and CentralLimitTheoremOQ01OQ02 into scope, making lemmas like Complex.sub_re and the parent's gaussianExponent directly accessible without qualification.
mathContext: $\psi(t) = i\mu t - \frac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2}$ encoded as $\texttt{ofReal}(\mu t) \cdot I - \texttt{ofReal}(\sigma^2 t^2/2) \in \mathbb{C}$

title: gaussianExponent at t = 0: Explicit simp Proof
content: This theorem re-proves ψ(0) = 0 with explicit simp unfolding of gaussianExponent, demonstrating the arithmetic path: μ·0 = 0 (mul_zero), then ofReal(0) = 0 (ofReal_zero), then 0·I = 0 (zero_mul), so ψ(0) = 0 − 0 = 0 (sub_self). The parent entry proved this the same way; this companion makes the simp steps visible and serves as the base for gaussianCharFn_at_zero.

title: Real and Imaginary Parts of the Gaussian Exponent
content:
gaussianExponent_re and gaussianExponent_im extract the two components of ψ(t) using the standard Complex simp set: Complex.sub_re/im for the subtraction, Complex.mul_re/im for the product with I, Complex.I_re = 0 and Complex.I_im = 1 for the imaginary unit, and Complex.ofReal_re/im for the embeddings. The arithmetic closes by ring.

The two components have fundamentally different roles: Re(ψ(t)) = −σ²t²/2 is negative-definite and causes |exp(ψ(t))| = exp(−σ²t²/2) to decay to 0 as |t| → ∞ — this is the 'damping' that ensures the Gaussian characteristic function is L²(ℝ). Im(ψ(t)) = μt produces the phase shift exp(iμt) corresponding to translation by μ in the spatial domain.

title: Pure Imaginary Case: Deterministic Drift Without Diffusion
content: When σ² = 0 the exponent reduces to ψ(t) = iμt, a purely imaginary number. The corresponding characteristic function exp(iμt) is the characteristic function of the Dirac delta distribution δ_μ — a deterministic constant μ. gaussianExponent_pure_imaginary proves this directly by simp on the definition (the ofReal(0) terms vanish). gaussianExponent_zero_sigma_re then immediately derives Re(ψ) = 0 from the general formula Re(ψ) = −σ²t²/2 = 0. This case represents pure rotation on the unit circle in ℂ, with |exp(ψ(t))| = 1 and no amplitude decay.
mathContext: $\sigma^2 = 0 \Rightarrow \psi(t) = i\mu t \in i\mathbb{R}$, $\quad e^{\psi(t)} = e^{i\mu t}$, $\quad |e^{\psi(t)}| = 1$ for all $t$

title: Conjugate Symmetry of the Gaussian Characteristic Function
content: The even/odd symmetry of the Gaussian exponent's components corresponds to conjugate symmetry φ(−t) = conj(φ(t)) of the characteristic function, which holds for all real-valued random variables. gaussianExponent_re_even shows Re(ψ(−t)) = Re(ψ(t)) since (−t)² = t² (even in t). gaussianExponent_im_odd shows Im(ψ(−t)) = −Im(ψ(t)) since μ(−t) = −μt (odd in t). Both reduce to ring goals after simp unfolding of the respective component lemmas. Together they imply exp(ψ(−t)) = conj(exp(ψ(t))), which reflects the Hermitian property of the Fourier transform applied to a real probability density.

title: Normalization: Characteristic Function = 1 at Origin
content: gaussianCharFn_at_zero proves exp(ψ(0)) = 1 via two steps: rewrite ψ(0) = 0 using gaussianExponent_zero, then apply Complex.exp_zero. This is the universal normalization of characteristic functions: φ(0) = E[e^{i·0·X}] = E[1] = 1 for any probability distribution. The property plays a key role in the CLT proof strategy: one verifies that the normalized characteristic functions φ_n(t) of (S_n − nμ)/(σ√n) converge pointwise to exp(−t²/2), uses normalization at 0 together with equicontinuity, and concludes distributional convergence to N(0,1) via Lévy's continuity theorem.
